She had watched her sister suffer week after week, burdened by a misery she had neither courage to discuss nor strength to hide. Now she saw an apparent peace of mind with a joy nobody else could equally share. If, as she trusted, it came from serious reflection, it must eventually lead to contentment and cheerfulness.

As they approached Barton, however, every field and tree recalled something particular and painful. Marianne grew quiet and thoughtful, turning her face away and gazing intently through the window. Elinor could neither wonder nor blame her. Helping her from the carriage, she saw that Marianne had been crying. The emotion was too natural to inspire anything less tender than pity, and its quietness deserved praise. Everything in her subsequent behaviour suggested a mind awakened to reasonable effort. The moment they entered the sitting room, Marianne looked firmly around, apparently determined to accustom herself at once to every object connected with Willoughby. She spoke little, but every sentence attempted cheerfulness. A sigh sometimes escaped, yet was always followed by a compensating smile. After dinner she tried the piano. The first music she saw, however, was an opera Willoughby had obtained for her, containing some of their favourite duets and bearing her name on the cover in his handwriting. That would not do. Shaking her head, she put it aside. After running her fingers over the keys for a minute, she complained that they were weak and closed the instrument. As she did so, however, she firmly declared that she would practise a great deal in future.

The next morning brought no weakening of these encouraging signs. Rest had strengthened body and mind alike. She looked and spoke with more genuine animation, anticipating Margaret's return and the restoration of their dear family circle. Their shared pursuits and cheerful companionship were, she said, the only happiness worth wishing for.

“When the weather settles and I have my strength back,” she said, “we shall take long walks together every day. We shall go to the farm beside the down and see how the children are getting on, to Sir John's new plantations at Barton Cross, and to Abbeyland. Often we shall visit the old Priory ruins and try to trace the foundations as far as we are told they once extended. I know we shall be happy. I know the summer will pass happily. I intend never to rise later than six, and from then until dinner I shall divide every minute between music and reading. My plan is formed: I mean to undertake serious study. I know our own library too well to use it for anything beyond amusement. But there are many worthwhile books at the Park, and more recent works I know I can borrow from Colonel Brandon. Reading only six hours a day, I shall gain a great deal of the knowledge I now lack within a year.”

Elinor respected a plan arising from such worthy intentions. Still, she smiled to see the same eager imagination which had carried Marianne to extremes of idle listlessness and selfish complaint now introducing excess into a scheme of sensible occupation and virtuous self-control. Her smile became a sigh when she remembered her unfulfilled promise to Willoughby. She feared she must communicate something that might unsettle Marianne again and destroy, at least temporarily, this promising prospect of peaceful activity. Wanting to postpone the painful moment, she decided to wait until her sister's health was stronger. But she made the resolution only to break it.

Marianne had been home two or three days before the weather became fine enough for someone recovering from illness to go out. At last a mild, pleasant morning encouraged both her desire and her mother's confidence. Leaning on Elinor's arm, she was permitted to walk in the lane outside the house for as long as she could without tiredness.

The sisters walked slowly, as Marianne's weakness required in exercise she had not attempted since her illness. They had gone only far enough for a full view of the hill behind the house—that important hill—when Marianne paused, looked towards it, and calmly said,
“There, just there”—she pointed with one hand—“on that jutting mound. That is where I fell, and where I first saw Willoughby.”
Her voice faded on his name, but she soon recovered it and continued.
“I am grateful that I can look at the place with so little pain. Shall we ever speak about it, Elinor?” She hesitated. “Or would it be wrong? I hope I _can_ talk about it now in the way I ought.”
Elinor gently encouraged her to speak freely.

“As for regret,” Marianne said, “I have finished with that, where _he_ is concerned. I do not want to tell you what my feelings for him were, but what they are _now_. If I could be satisfied about one thing, if I could believe that he was not _always_ playing a part, not _always_ deceiving me—and, above all, if I could be certain he was never as _terribly_ wicked as I have sometimes feared since hearing about that unfortunate girl—”
She stopped. Elinor treasured the words with joy and answered,
“If you could be sure of that, you think you would find peace?”

“Yes. My peace depends on it in two ways. It is terrible to suspect someone who meant what _he_ meant to _me_ of such intentions. But what does that make me in my own eyes? In my position, what but shamefully unguarded love could have exposed me to—”
“How, then,” her sister asked, “would you explain his behaviour towards you?”
“I would think him—oh, how gladly I would think him—only changeable, very, very changeable.”
Elinor said nothing further. She was considering whether to begin her story immediately or wait until Marianne was stronger. For several minutes they moved slowly on in silence.
“I do not wish him too much happiness,” Marianne said at last with a sigh, “when I wish his private reflections no more painful than mine. Those will make him suffer enough.”
“Are you comparing your behaviour with his own?”
“No. I compare it with what it should have been. I compare it with your behaviour.”
“Our circumstances have been very different.”

“Less different than our conduct. Dearest Elinor, don't let your kindness defend what I know your judgement must condemn. Illness has made me think. It gave me time and quiet for serious reflection. Long before I was well enough to talk, I could think perfectly clearly. I looked back. From the beginning of our acquaintance with him last autumn, I saw in my own behaviour only a succession of recklessness towards myself and unkindness towards others. I saw that my feelings had prepared my suffering, and that my lack of courage in bearing it had nearly taken me to the grave. I knew I had brought the illness entirely on myself by neglecting my health in ways I understood, even then, to be wrong. If I had died, I would have destroyed myself. I did not know my danger until it had passed. But remembering what those reflections made me feel, I wonder that I recovered. I wonder that my intense desire to live, to have time to make amends to God and to all of you, did not kill me at once. If I had died, what particular misery I would have left you in—my nurse, my friend, my sister! You had seen all the irritable selfishness of those last days, heard every complaint of my heart. How would I have lived in _your_ memory? And our mother! How could you have comforted her? I cannot express how deeply I despised myself. Whenever I looked back, I found some neglected duty or indulged fault. Everyone seemed to have been hurt by me. I had repaid Mrs. Jennings's constant kindness with ungrateful contempt. I had been rude and unjust to the Middletons, Palmers, Steeles, even the most ordinary acquaintances. I had shut my heart against their good qualities and let their very attention irritate me. To John and Fanny—yes, even them, little as they deserve—I had given less than I owed. But you, above everyone, even above our mother, had been wronged. I alone knew your heart and its sorrow. What did that knowledge lead me to? No compassion that helped either of us. Your example was before me, but to what purpose? Did I consider you and your comfort more? Did I imitate your patience, or ease your restrictions by taking any share in the ordinary courtesies and particular expressions of gratitude you had been left to manage alone? No. Knowing you unhappy, I still refused every effort of duty or friendship, just as I had when I thought you content. I scarcely allowed that sorrow existed outside myself. I mourned only _the_ heart that had abandoned and wronged me, leaving you, whom I claimed to love without limit, to suffer on my account.”

Her rapid stream of self-reproach stopped. Eager to comfort her, though too honest to flatter, Elinor immediately offered the praise and support her openness and remorse deserved. Marianne pressed her hand and replied,

“You are very kind. The future must prove me. I have made my plan. If I can keep to it, I shall control my feelings and improve my temper. They will no longer distress others or torment me. From now on I shall live entirely for my family. You, our mother, and Margaret must be my whole world, sharing all my affection between you. I shall never again feel the smallest wish to leave you or my home. If I enter other company, it will only be to show that my spirit is humbled, my heart improved, and that I can perform life's courtesies and smaller duties gently and patiently. As for Willoughby, it would be foolish to say I shall soon forget him, or ever forget him. No change of circumstances or opinion can erase his memory. But I shall govern it and keep it in check through religion, reason, and constant occupation.”
She paused, then added quietly, “If only I could know _his_ heart, everything would be easier.”

Elinor had been weighing the wisdom of telling her story at once for some time, without coming any nearer a decision. Hearing this, she realised that if reflection achieved nothing, determination must do everything. She soon found herself approaching the subject.

She hoped she told it tactfully. She prepared her anxious listener carefully, explained simply and honestly the chief arguments in Willoughby's defence, gave his repentance its due, and softened only his declarations of continuing love. Marianne said nothing. She trembled, stared at the ground, and her lips grew paler than illness had left them. A thousand questions rose in her heart, but she dared ask none. She caught every syllable with breathless eagerness. Without knowing it, she gripped Elinor's hand tightly, while tears covered her cheeks.

Fearing that Marianne was tired, Elinor led her home. Until they reached the cottage door, she spoke only of Willoughby and their conversation. She could easily guess Marianne's curiosity, though no question expressed it, and supplied careful details of every word and look where such detail could safely be given. Once inside, Marianne kissed her gratefully. Through her tears she could just manage to say two words, “Tell Mama,” before leaving her sister and going slowly upstairs. Elinor would not disturb so reasonable a wish for solitude. Anxiously imagining its effect, and resolved to reopen the subject herself if Marianne did not, she entered the sitting room to carry out her sister's request.

chapters.title: Chapter 47
paragraphs: Mrs. Dashwood was moved by the defence of her former favourite. She was glad to see him cleared of some of the guilt attributed to him, felt sorry for him, and wished him happy. But the old feelings could not return. Nothing could restore him to Marianne with his promises unbroken and his character unstained. Nothing could erase the knowledge of what he had made her suffer, or remove his guilt towards Eliza. He could not regain Mrs. Dashwood's former esteem, therefore, or threaten Colonel Brandon's prospects.

Had Mrs. Dashwood heard Willoughby's account directly, as Elinor had, witnessed his distress, and felt the influence of his face and manner, she would probably have pitied him more. But Elinor could neither reproduce in her retelling the feelings first aroused in herself, nor wished to do so. Reflection had steadied her judgement and moderated her estimate of what Willoughby deserved. She therefore wanted to state only the plain truth, presenting the facts fairness to his character required, without tender embellishments to mislead the imagination.

That evening, when all three were together, Marianne voluntarily began to speak of him again. The effort was evident in the restless thoughtfulness that had occupied her for some time, in her rising colour as she spoke, and in her unsteady voice.
“I want to assure you both,” she said, “that I see everything as you would wish me to see it.”

Mrs. Dashwood would have interrupted at once with tender reassurance, but Elinor earnestly signalled her to remain silent. She wanted to hear Marianne's own uninfluenced judgement. Marianne slowly continued.

“What Elinor told me this morning is a great relief. I have now heard exactly what I wanted to hear.” Her voice failed for a few moments. Recovering, she added more calmly, “I am quite satisfied now. I wish nothing changed. I could never have been happy with him after learning all this, as sooner or later I must have done. I could have felt neither trust nor respect. Nothing could have removed it from my mind.”

“I know, I know!” her mother exclaimed. “Happy with a man who lived so immorally! Someone who so wounded the peace of our dearest friend, the best of men! No, my Marianne's heart could never find happiness with such a man. Her conscience, her sensitive conscience, would have felt everything her husband's ought to feel.”
Marianne sighed and said again, “I wish nothing changed.”

“You see it exactly as a good heart and sound judgement must,” Elinor said. “And I expect you understand, as I do, that this is not the only reason to believe your marriage would have brought many certain troubles and disappointments, with little support from a love on his side far less certain. If you had married, you would always have been poor. He admits his own extravagance. His whole conduct shows that self-denial is a word he scarcely understands. His demands and your inexperience, combined with a small, very small income, would have caused difficulties no _less_ painful because you had never known or imagined them before. Your own honour and honesty would, I know, have made you attempt every economy you could once you understood the situation. Perhaps, while your saving reduced only your own comforts, you would have been allowed to practise it. But beyond that—and how little could even your greatest efforts alone have done to halt a ruin begun before the marriage?—if you had reasonably tried to reduce _his_ pleasures, might you not have weakened his love instead of persuading such selfish feelings to agree? Might he not have regretted the marriage that brought him those difficulties?”
Marianne's lips trembled. “Selfish?” she repeated, in a tone that asked, “Do you really believe he is selfish?”

“His entire behaviour, from beginning to end, rested on selfishness,” Elinor answered. “It first made him play with your feelings. When he began to love you himself, it made him postpone admitting it. Finally, it took him away from Barton. In every action, his own enjoyment or comfort was the principle that governed him.”
“That is very true. _My_ happiness was never his purpose.”

“Now he regrets what he did,” Elinor continued. “Why? Because it has not worked out well for himself. It has not made him happy. His finances are secure; he suffers no trouble there. He thinks only that he has married a woman less sweet-tempered than you. But does that prove he would have been happy with you? The difficulties would have been different. He would have suffered the financial distress which, now it is removed, he counts as nothing. He could not have complained of his wife's temper, but would always have been short of money, always poor. Probably he would soon have considered the countless comforts of an unburdened estate and a good income far more important, even to happiness at home, than merely having a pleasant-tempered wife.”
“I don't doubt it,” Marianne said. “There is nothing for me to regret except my own foolishness.”
“Say rather your mother's lack of judgement, my child,” Mrs. Dashwood said. “_She_ must take the blame.”

Marianne would not let her continue. Satisfied that each recognised her own mistake, Elinor wanted to avoid dwelling on the past in ways that might weaken her sister's spirits. She therefore immediately returned to their first subject.

“I think _one_ conclusion can fairly be drawn from the whole story: every difficulty Willoughby has suffered began with his first wrongdoing, his treatment of Eliza Williams. That offence was the source of every lesser one and of all his present unhappiness.”

Marianne agreed with deep feeling. Her mother took the remark as an opportunity to list Colonel Brandon's sufferings and merits with all the warmth friendship and purpose could jointly inspire. Marianne, however, did not seem to hear much of it.

As Elinor had expected, during the next two or three days Marianne no longer gained strength as quickly. But her determination remained firm and she still tried to appear cheerful and at ease. Her sister could therefore safely trust time to restore her health.

Margaret returned, reuniting the whole family in the quiet of the cottage. If they did not pursue their usual studies with quite the energy of their first days at Barton, they at least planned to pursue them energetically in future.

Elinor became impatient for news of Edward. Since leaving London, she had heard nothing of him, no fresh plans, not even certain information about where he was living. Marianne's illness had occasioned several letters between Elinor and John. His first included this sentence: “We know nothing of our unfortunate Edward, and cannot inquire about so forbidden a subject, but assume he is still at Oxford.” That was all the correspondence told her. The later letters did not even mention his name. She would not, however, remain ignorant of his actions for long.
One morning their manservant was sent to Exeter on business. Later, while waiting at table, he answered his mistress's questions about the result of his errand, then volunteered this information.
“I suppose you know, ma'am, that Mr. Ferrars has got married.”

Marianne started violently and fixed her eyes on Elinor. Seeing her turn pale, she fell back in her chair in a fit of distress. As Mrs. Dashwood answered the servant, her own eyes had instinctively turned the same way. Elinor's expression shocked her by revealing the depth of her suffering. A moment later, equally distressed by Marianne's condition, she did not know which daughter needed her most.

The servant noticed only that Miss Marianne had become unwell. Sensibly, he called a maid, who helped Mrs. Dashwood support her into the next room. Marianne was somewhat better by then. Leaving her with Margaret and the maid, their mother returned to Elinor. Still deeply shaken, she had recovered enough reason and voice to begin asking Thomas where he had obtained the news. Mrs. Dashwood immediately took over the questioning, letting Elinor hear the information without the effort of asking for it.
“Who told you Mr. Ferrars had married, Thomas?”

“I saw him myself this morning in Exeter, ma'am, and his wife too, Miss Steele as was. They were stopped in a chaise outside the New London Inn. I went there with a message from Sally at the Park to her brother, one of the post-boys. As I passed the carriage, I looked up and recognised the younger Miss Steele straight away. I took off my hat. She knew me, called me over, and asked after you and the young ladies, especially Miss Marianne. She told me to give you her compliments and Mr. Ferrars's, their best compliments and respects. They were sorry not to have time to come and see you, but they had to hurry on. They were going further down the country for a little while. When they came back, though, they would be sure to visit.”
“But did she say that she was married, Thomas?”

“Yes, ma'am. She smiled and said she'd changed her name since she was last in these parts. She was always a friendly, freely spoken young lady, with very civil manners. So I took the liberty of congratulating her.”
“Was Mr. Ferrars there in the carriage with her?”
“Yes, ma'am. I just saw him leaning back inside, but he didn't look up. He was never a gentleman who talked a great deal.”
Elinor's heart readily explained why he had not come forward. Her mother probably found the same explanation.
“Was anybody else travelling in the carriage?”
“No, ma'am. Only the two of them.”
“Do you know where they had come from?”
“Straight from London, so Miss Lucy—Mrs. Ferrars—told me herself.”
“And are they travelling further west?”
“Yes, ma'am, but not for long. They'll soon be coming back, and then they'll be certain to call here.”

Mrs. Dashwood looked at Elinor, who knew better than to expect them. The message was entirely characteristic of Lucy, and she felt certain Edward would never come near them. Quietly, she told her mother that they were probably going to Mr. Pratt's, near Plymouth.
Thomas appeared to have finished his news. Elinor looked as though she wanted more.
“Did you see them leave before you came away?”
“No, ma'am. The horses were just being brought out, but I couldn't wait any longer. I was afraid I would be late.”
“Did Mrs. Ferrars seem well?”
“Yes, ma'am. She said she was very well. I've always thought her a very pretty young lady, and she seemed extremely contented.”

Mrs. Dashwood could think of nothing else to ask. Thomas and the tablecloth, equally unnecessary now, were soon dismissed. Marianne had already sent word that she would eat no more. Her mother and Elinor had lost their appetites too. Margaret might consider herself fortunate that, through all the distress her sisters had lately suffered and all their frequent reasons to neglect meals, she had never before been obliged to miss her dinner.

After dessert and wine were set out, Mrs. Dashwood and Elinor were left alone. For a long time they sat together in matching thoughtfulness and silence. Their mother dared risk no remark and offered no consolation. She now realised her mistake in trusting Elinor's account of her feelings. Rightly, she concluded that her daughter had deliberately softened everything to spare her additional distress while she was suffering for Marianne. Elinor's careful consideration had misled her into believing that the attachment she had once understood so well was much slighter than she formerly thought, or than it now proved to be. She feared that this belief had made her unfair, inattentive, even almost unkind to Elinor. Marianne's more openly expressed and immediately visible sorrow had absorbed too much of her tenderness. She had forgotten that her other daughter might suffer nearly as much, certainly with less responsibility for it and greater courage.

chapters.title: Chapter 48
paragraphs: Elinor now learnt the difference between expecting an unhappy event, however certain one tells oneself it is, and knowing it has happened. She discovered that, despite herself, while Edward remained unmarried she had always entertained a hope that something would prevent his marriage to Lucy. Some decision of his own, some intervention by friends, or some better prospect for Lucy might have appeared to make everyone happier. But now he was married. She blamed her heart for the hidden hope that made the news so much more painful.

At first she was a little surprised that he had married so quickly, before, as she supposed, he could have been ordained and therefore before taking possession of the living. But she soon understood how likely Lucy was, in her concern for her own interests and haste to secure him, to ignore everything except the risk of delay. They were married, married in London, and now hurrying to her uncle's. What had Edward felt at coming within four miles of Barton, seeing her mother's servant, and hearing Lucy's message?

She supposed they would soon settle at Delaford. Delaford: a place in which so much combined to interest her, which she wanted to know and yet wished to avoid. Instantly she pictured them in their parsonage. Lucy would be an energetic, calculating housekeeper, combining the wish for a smart appearance with the strictest economy, ashamed to have half her saving practices suspected. Every thought would pursue her own interest, every attention seek the favour of Colonel Brandon, Mrs. Jennings, and each wealthy friend. In Edward she did not know what she saw or wished to see. Happy or unhappy, no picture satisfied her. She turned from every imagined version of him.

Elinor hoped that someone they knew in London would write to announce the marriage and give more details. But day followed day without letter or news. She could not be sure anybody was at fault, yet blamed every absent friend. They were all thoughtless or lazy.
“When will you write to Colonel Brandon, Mama?” she asked, driven by impatience for something, anything, to be happening.
“I wrote last week, my dear. I rather expect to see him before hearing from him again. I urged him warmly to come and should not be surprised if he walked in today, tomorrow, or any day.”
That was something gained, something to anticipate. Colonel Brandon _must_ have at least some news to tell.

She had scarcely decided this when a man on horseback caught her eye through the window. He stopped at their gate. A gentleman—Colonel Brandon himself! Now she would hear more, and she trembled at the prospect. But it was _not_ Colonel Brandon. Neither his height nor his bearing matched. If such a thing were possible, she would have to call him Edward. She looked again. He had just dismounted. There could be no mistake: it _was_ Edward. She moved away and sat down. “He has come from Mr. Pratt's expressly to see us. I _will_ be calm. I _will_ control myself.”

A moment later she realised the others had discovered their mistake too. Her mother and Marianne changed colour, looked towards her, and whispered a few words together. She would have given anything to speak and make them understand that she wanted no coldness, no slight, in their treatment of him. But no words came. She had to leave everything to their judgement.
Nobody spoke aloud. They waited silently for their visitor. His footsteps sounded on the gravel path. A moment later he was in the passage; another, and he stood before them.

Even Elinor could not consider him too happy as he entered. He was pale with agitation, and looked afraid of his welcome, as though conscious he deserved no kind reception. But Mrs. Dashwood, hoping to follow the wishes of the daughter whose feelings her affectionate heart now intended to consult in everything, greeted him with forced pleasantness. She gave him her hand and offered her congratulations.

He blushed and stammered an incomprehensible reply. Elinor's lips had moved along with her mother's. Once the moment had passed, she wished she too had shaken hands with him. It was too late now. Trying to look open and friendly, she sat down again and talked about the weather.

Marianne had withdrawn as far out of sight as possible to hide her distress. Margaret understood part of the situation, though not all. Believing dignity required it, she sat as far from him as she could and said nothing at all.

When Elinor had finished expressing pleasure in the dry weather, a dreadful silence followed. Mrs. Dashwood ended it by feeling obliged to hope he had left Mrs. Ferrars in good health. He hurriedly answered that he had.
Silence followed again.
Determined to make an effort, though frightened by the sound of her own voice, Elinor now asked,
“Is Mrs. Ferrars staying at Longstaple?”
“At Longstaple?” he repeated in surprise. “No. My mother is still in London.”
“I meant,” Elinor said, picking up some work from the table, “to ask after Mrs. _Edward_ Ferrars.”
She dared not raise her eyes. Her mother and Marianne both looked at him. He coloured, seemed confused, glanced uncertainly about, and after some hesitation replied,
“Perhaps you mean—my brother—you mean Mrs.—Mrs. _Robert_ Ferrars.”

“Mrs. Robert Ferrars!” Marianne and her mother repeated in utter astonishment. Elinor could not speak, but even _her_ eyes fixed on him with the same eager wonder. He got up and went to the window, apparently at a loss what to do. Picking up a pair of scissors lying there, he began cutting their sheath to pieces as he spoke, damaging both it and the scissors. In a hurried voice he said,
“Perhaps you don't know. Perhaps you haven't heard that my brother recently married—to the younger—to Miss Lucy Steele.”
Everyone echoed his words in indescribable amazement except Elinor. She remained sitting with her head bent down over her work, so agitated that she scarcely knew where she was.
“Yes,” he said, “they were married last week. They are at Dawlish now.”

Elinor could remain seated no longer. She almost ran from the room. As soon as the door closed, she burst into tears of joy which at first seemed as though they would never stop. Until then, Edward had looked anywhere except at her. He saw her hurry away, and perhaps saw, or even heard, her emotion. Immediately afterwards he sank into thought so deeply that no comment, question, or affectionate remark from Mrs. Dashwood reached him. At last he left without a word and walked towards the village. The others remained astonished and bewildered at a change in his circumstances so sudden and extraordinary. They had nothing but their own guesses to explain it.

chapters.title: Chapter 49
paragraphs: However inexplicable the circumstances of his release seemed to the family, Edward was certainly free, and everyone could readily predict how he would use that freedom. Having enjoyed for more than four years the blessings of _one_ rash engagement made without his mother's consent, he could hardly be expected, when _that_ failed, to do anything less than enter another immediately.

His purpose at Barton was simple enough: he had come to ask Elinor to marry him. Since he was not entirely inexperienced in asking such a question, it might seem strange that he should feel as uncomfortable as he did, and need so much encouragement and fresh air.

How quickly walking supplied the necessary courage, how soon an opportunity arose, what he said, and how she received it need not be described in detail. It is enough to say that when they sat down to dinner at four, about three hours after his arrival, he had won his lady and her mother's consent. He was one of the happiest men alive, not merely in a lover's ecstatic declaration, but in sober fact. His situation was unusually joyful. More than the ordinary triumph of accepted love filled his heart and lifted his spirits. Without blame to himself, he had been freed from an engagement that had long made him miserable, to a woman he had long ceased to love. At once he had gained certainty with another, a prospect he must have regarded almost hopelessly from the moment he began to desire it. He had moved not from doubt or uncertainty to happiness, but from misery. The change showed in a spontaneous, generous, grateful cheerfulness his friends had never seen in him before.
His heart was open to Elinor now. He confessed every weakness and mistake, treating his first boyish love for Lucy with all the philosophical dignity of twenty-four.

“It was a foolish, idle fancy,” he said, “born of not knowing the world and having nothing to do. If my mother had given me an active profession when I left Mr. Pratt at eighteen, I think—indeed, I am certain—it would never have happened. I left Longstaple believing my preference for his niece impossible to overcome. But any occupation, any purpose to fill my time and keep me away for a few months, would soon have made me outgrow that imagined attachment, especially with the wider experience of society it would necessarily have brought. Instead, no profession was chosen for me, and I was not allowed to choose one myself. I returned home to complete idleness. For the first year I did not even have the nominal occupation of belonging to a university; I did not enter Oxford until nineteen. I had nothing in the world to do except imagine myself in love. My mother did not make home comfortable in every respect. My brother was neither friend nor companion, and I disliked meeting new people. It was therefore natural to visit Longstaple often, where I always felt at home and knew I was welcome. I spent most of the year between eighteen and nineteen there. Lucy seemed everything kind and obliging. She was pretty too—at least I thought so _then_. I had seen so few other women that I could make no comparison and notice no faults. Taking everything into account, I hope that, foolish as our engagement was and has since proved in every way, it was not at the time either unnatural or inexcusable foolishness.”

The transformation a few hours had made in the Dashwoods' minds and happiness was so great that it promised all of them the pleasure of a sleepless night. Too happy to be comfortable, Mrs. Dashwood did not know how to love Edward or praise Elinor enough, how to express sufficient gratitude for his release without hurting his delicacy, or how to give them freedom to talk alone while still enjoying the sight and company of both as much as she wished.
Marianne could express _her_ happiness only in tears. Comparisons arose, and regrets followed. Her joy was as sincere as her love for Elinor, but it brought her neither liveliness nor words.

As for Elinor, how can _her_ feelings be described? From the moment she learnt that Lucy had married someone else and Edward was free, to the moment he justified the hopes that instantly followed, she felt everything in turn except calm. But once that second moment had passed, every doubt and anxiety removed, she compared her position with what it had so recently been. He was honourably free of his former engagement and had immediately used that freedom to propose to her, declaring a love as tender and constant as she had ever believed. Her own happiness overwhelmed her. Though the human mind is fortunately quick to grow familiar with any improvement, several hours were needed before her spirits settled or her heart knew any peace.

Edward was now to stay at the cottage for at least a week. Whatever other claims existed, no less time could be given to enjoying Elinor's company, or could cover even half what they had to say about past, present, and future. A few hours of the hard work of uninterrupted conversation may exhaust more subjects than any two reasonable people truly share, but lovers are different. For _them_, no subject is finished, no communication even made, until it has been repeated at least twenty times.

Lucy's marriage remained a constant and reasonable source of wonder to everyone, and naturally formed one of the lovers' earliest topics. Elinor's particular knowledge of both parties made it seem in every respect one of the most extraordinary, inexplicable events she had heard of. How had they come together? What attraction could make Robert marry a woman whose beauty she had heard him discuss without admiration—a woman already engaged to his brother, for whose sake that brother had been cast off by his family? She could not understand it. Her heart found it delightful, her imagination even ridiculous, but her reason and judgement found it an absolute puzzle.

Edward could only suggest that they might first have met entirely by chance, and that one person's vanity, worked upon by the other's flattery, had gradually led to everything else. Elinor remembered Robert's account in Harley Street of what his intervention might have achieved for Edward if he had been consulted soon enough. She repeated it.

“_That_ is exactly like Robert,” Edward said at once. Then he added, “Perhaps _that_ was in _his_ mind when they first became acquainted. Lucy too may initially have wanted only to obtain his help for me. Other plans could have developed afterwards.”

But he could no more explain how long it had been going on than Elinor could. Since leaving London, he had chosen to remain at Oxford, where all his news of Lucy came from her own letters. Until the very last they had arrived as often and sounded as affectionate as ever. No suspicion had prepared him for what followed. When it finally came in a letter from Lucy herself, he believed he had been half stunned for some time by the mixture of astonishment, horror, and joy at such a release. He handed the letter to Elinor.

“DEAR SIR, “Being certain that I lost your love long ago, I considered myself free to give mine to someone else. I do not doubt that I shall be as happy with him as I once thought I might be with you, but I refuse to accept a hand when the heart belongs to another. I sincerely wish you happiness in your choice. It will not be my fault if we do not always remain good friends, as our close relationship now requires. I can safely say I feel no ill will towards you, and am sure you are too generous to do anything against us. Your brother has won all my affection. Since we could not live without each other, we have just returned from the altar and are on our way to Dawlish for a few weeks. Your dear brother is very curious to see it. I thought I would first trouble you with these few lines, and shall always remain,
“Your sincere well-wisher, friend, and sister, “LUCY FERRARS.
“I have burned all your letters and will return your portrait at the first opportunity. Please destroy my scribbles. You are very welcome, however, to keep the ring containing my hair.”
Elinor read the letter and handed it back without comment.

“I won't ask your opinion of its composition,” Edward said. “In former days I would not for anything have let _you_ see a letter of hers. In a sister it is bad enough, but in a wife! How I have blushed over those pages. Since the first six months of our foolish—affair—I think this is the only letter whose contents have compensated me for its style.”

“However it happened,” Elinor said after a pause, “they are certainly married. Your mother has brought a very fitting punishment on herself. By making Robert independent out of resentment against you, she enabled him to choose for himself. She has effectively bribed one son with a thousand a year to do exactly what she disinherited the other for intending. I suppose Robert's marriage to Lucy will hurt her scarcely less than yours would have done.”
“It will hurt her more, because Robert was always her favourite. It will hurt more, and for precisely the same reason she will forgive him much sooner.”

Edward did not know how matters stood between them now, since he had attempted no communication with any of his family. Within twenty-four hours of receiving Lucy's letter, he had left Oxford with only one object in mind: the shortest route to Barton. He had no time to form any plan of conduct not closely connected with that road. Until he knew his fate with Elinor, he could do nothing. His haste in discovering _that_ fate suggests that, despite his former jealousy of Colonel Brandon, his modest estimate of his own merits, and his polite expressions of doubt, he did not altogether expect a cruel reception. Still, his role was to say that he _did_, and he said it very prettily. What he might say about it a year later must be left to the imagination of husbands and wives.

Elinor had no doubt that Lucy's message through Thomas was deliberately intended to deceive, a final flourish of malice against Edward as she left him. Now thoroughly informed about her character, Edward had no hesitation in believing her capable of the pettiest deliberate unkindness. Long before meeting Elinor, he had recognised Lucy's ignorance and a lack of generosity and breadth in some of her opinions, but attributed both to her lack of education. Until her final letter, he had always believed her a well-meaning, good-hearted girl who loved him deeply. Only that belief could have kept him from ending an engagement that had caused constant anxiety and regret long before its discovery exposed him to his mother's anger.

“When my mother disowned me,” he said, “and I seemed without a friend to help me, I thought it my duty, regardless of my feelings, to let Lucy choose whether the engagement continued. In circumstances like those, where there seemed to be nothing in the world to attract anyone's greed or vanity, how could I imagine any motive but selfless love when she so warmly insisted on sharing whatever fate awaited me? Even now I cannot understand what she wanted, or what advantage she imagined in remaining bound to a man she did not care for and who possessed only two thousand pounds. She could not foresee Colonel Brandon offering me a living.”

“No. But she could hope something would happen in your favour, or that your family might eventually relent. In any case, remaining engaged cost her nothing: she has proved it restricted neither her wishes nor her actions. The connection was respectable and probably made her important among her friends. If nothing better appeared, marrying _you_ would suit her better than remaining single.”
Naturally, Edward was immediately convinced that nothing could be more normal than Lucy's behaviour, or more obvious than her motive.
Elinor scolded him for spending so much time at Norland when he must have known his feelings had changed, with all the severity women usually show towards imprudence that flatters themselves.
“Your conduct was certainly wrong,” she said. “Leaving aside my own belief, it encouraged all our relations to imagine and expect _something_ which, in your circumstances _then_, could never happen.”
He could plead only ignorance of his own heart and misplaced confidence in the strength of his engagement.

“I was foolish enough to think that, because I had _pledged_ myself to another, being with you could pose no danger. Knowing I was engaged would keep my heart as secure and faithful as my honour. I knew I admired you, but called it friendship. Until I began comparing you and Lucy, I did not realise how far I had gone. After that, I suppose I _was_ wrong to stay so much in Sussex. My arguments for doing so were no better than these: the danger is mine alone; I am hurting nobody but myself.”
Elinor smiled at him and shook her head.

Edward was glad to hear Colonel Brandon was expected at the cottage. He genuinely wanted to know him better and to show that he no longer resented being given the Delaford living. “As things stand,” he said, “after the ungracious way I thanked him, he must think I have never forgiven him for offering it.”

_Now_ Edward was himself amazed that he had not yet visited the place. Until then he had taken so little interest that everything he knew about the house, garden, church land, parish boundaries, state of the soil, and value of the tithes came from Elinor. She had listened to Colonel Brandon say so much, and listened so attentively, that she knew the subject thoroughly.

Only one question now remained, one difficulty to overcome. Love had brought them together with the warm approval of their true friends. Their close knowledge of each other seemed to guarantee happiness. They only lacked something to live on. Edward had two thousand pounds and Elinor one thousand. Together with the Delaford living, that was all they could claim, since Mrs. Dashwood could not possibly advance anything. Neither was quite enough in love to believe three hundred and fifty pounds a year would supply life's comforts.

Edward retained some hope that his mother might become more favourable towards him, and relied on _that_ for the rest of their income. Elinor had no such expectation. He still could not marry Miss Morton, and his choosing Elinor had been described in Mrs. Ferrars's flattering language as merely a lesser evil than choosing Lucy Steele. She feared Robert's offence would achieve nothing beyond making Fanny richer.

About four days after Edward arrived, Colonel Brandon appeared, completing Mrs. Dashwood's satisfaction and giving her, for the first time at Barton, the distinction of more guests than her house could accommodate. Edward kept the privilege of having arrived first. The Colonel walked each night to his old rooms at the Park, usually returning early enough to interrupt the lovers' first private conversation before breakfast.

Three weeks at Delaford, with little to do in the evenings except calculate the difference between thirty-six and seventeen, had brought him to Barton in spirits that needed every improvement in Marianne's appearance, every kindness in her welcome, and every encouragement from her mother to become cheerful. Among such friends and such flattering attention, however, he revived. No rumour of Lucy's marriage had reached him; he knew nothing of the events. His first hours were consequently spent listening and wondering. Mrs. Dashwood explained everything, giving him fresh reason to rejoice in what he had done for Edward, since it had ultimately advanced Elinor's happiness.

It would be quite unnecessary to say that the gentlemen's regard for one another increased with their acquaintance; it could hardly have done otherwise. Their similar principles, intelligence, temperaments, and ways of thinking would probably have made them friends without any further attraction. But being in love with two sisters who loved each other made their mutual regard immediate and inevitable, instead of leaving it to time and judgement.

The letters from London which, a few days earlier, would have thrilled every nerve in Elinor's body now arrived to be read with more amusement than agitation. Mrs. Jennings related the astonishing story, expressed her honest anger at the faithless girl, and poured out pity for poor Edward. She was sure he had adored the worthless hussy and was now, by all accounts, nearly heartbroken at Oxford. “I think nothing was ever done so secretly,” she continued. “Only two days before, Lucy spent a couple of hours with me. Nobody suspected anything, not even Nancy. Poor soul, she came crying the next day, terrified of Mrs. Ferrars and not knowing how to get to Plymouth. It seems Lucy borrowed all her money before going off to marry, to make a show with it, we suppose. Nancy had not seven shillings left. I was very glad to give her five guineas to reach Exeter, where she means to stay three or four weeks with Mrs. Burgess—in hopes, as I tell her, of meeting the Doctor again. I must say Lucy's unkindness in not taking her sister along in the chaise is worst of all. Poor Mr. Edward! I cannot stop thinking of him. You must invite him to Barton, and Miss Marianne must try to comfort him.”

John Dashwood wrote more solemnly. Mrs. Ferrars was the most unfortunate woman alive; poor Fanny had suffered agonies of feeling. He regarded their survival under such a blow with grateful astonishment. Robert's offence was unforgivable, Lucy's infinitely worse. Neither name must ever be mentioned to Mrs. Ferrars again. Even if she could later be persuaded to forgive her son, his wife would never be acknowledged as her daughter or permitted in her presence. The secrecy was reasonably treated as making the crime enormously worse: had anyone suspected, proper measures would certainly have been taken to prevent the marriage. He asked Elinor to share his regret that Lucy had not married Edward instead of spreading misery further through the family. He continued:

“Mrs. Ferrars has not yet mentioned Edward, which does not surprise us. But to our great astonishment, we have had no letter from him about this. Perhaps fear of giving offence keeps him silent. I shall therefore write to Oxford suggesting that his sister and I think a suitably submissive letter, perhaps addressed to Fanny and shown by her to their mother, might be well received. We all know the tenderness of Mrs. Ferrars's heart and that nothing matters more to her than being on good terms with her children.”
This paragraph mattered to Edward's prospects and decisions. It persuaded him to attempt a reconciliation, though not exactly in the way John and Fanny recommended.

“A suitably submissive letter!” he repeated. “Do they want me to ask my mother's pardon for Robert's ingratitude towards _her_ and dishonourable treatment of _me_? I cannot submit. These events have made me neither humble nor repentant. They have made me very happy, but that would not interest them. I know no submission it _would_ be proper for me to make.”

“You can certainly ask forgiveness,” Elinor said, “because you have offended her. And I think you may _now_ venture to express some regret for ever forming the engagement that brought her anger upon you.”
He admitted that he could.
“Then, once she has forgiven you, perhaps a little humility might be useful when admitting to a second engagement almost as rash in _her_ eyes as the first.”

He could find no objection to this, but still resisted writing a submissive letter. He declared himself much more willing to make humiliating concessions aloud than on paper. To make it easier, they therefore decided he should go to London instead of writing to Fanny, and personally ask her to intercede for him. “If they really _do_ help bring about a reconciliation,” Marianne said in her new spirit of fair-mindedness, “I shall believe that even John and Fanny are not entirely without good qualities.”

After Colonel Brandon had stayed only three or four days, the two men left Barton together. They would go straight to Delaford so that Edward could see his future home and help his patron and friend decide what improvements were needed. From there, after remaining for a couple of nights, Edward was to continue on his journey to London.

chapters.title: Chapter 50
paragraphs: Mrs. Ferrars resisted for a suitable length of time, with exactly the force and firmness needed to save her from the accusation she always seemed most afraid of: that she was too kind. Edward was then allowed into her presence and declared to be her son once more.

The composition of her family had lately changed with remarkable frequency. For many years she had possessed two sons; but Edward’s crime, and his consequent extinction a few weeks earlier, had deprived her of one. Robert’s similar extinction had then left her without any sons for a fortnight; and now, with Edward restored to life, she had one again.

Yet even though he had permission to live again, Edward could not feel sure of remaining alive until he had disclosed his present engagement. He feared that announcing it might bring on a sudden change in his condition and carry him off as quickly as before. He therefore made the disclosure with anxious caution, and she heard him with a calm he had not expected. Mrs. Ferrars first made the entirely reasonable attempt to argue him out of marrying Miss Dashwood, using every argument she could command. With Miss Morton, she told him, he would acquire a wife of higher rank and greater wealth. She reinforced the point by observing that Miss Morton was a nobleman’s daughter with thirty thousand pounds, whereas Miss Dashwood was merely the daughter of an untitled gentleman with no more than _three_ thousand. But when she discovered that he fully acknowledged the accuracy of her account without showing the slightest inclination to act on it, past experience taught her that submission was the wisest course. Accordingly, after a delay sufficiently ungracious to satisfy the claims of her dignity and remove every suspicion of goodwill, she issued her permission for Edward and Elinor to marry.

The next question was what she would undertake to contribute to their income. Here it became quite clear that although Edward was now her only son, he was by no means her eldest. Robert’s thousand pounds a year could not be taken back; yet she raised not the smallest objection to Edward’s becoming a clergyman for an income of two hundred and fifty pounds at most. Nor did she promise him anything, either immediately or in the future, beyond the ten thousand pounds she had given Fanny on her marriage.

This, however, was all Edward and Elinor wanted, and more than they had expected. Mrs. Ferrars herself, with her evasive excuses, seemed to be the only person astonished that she was not giving them more.

They now had the certainty of an income fully adequate to their needs. Once Edward had taken possession of the living, they had only to wait for the house to be ready. Colonel Brandon, eager to make Elinor comfortable, was carrying out substantial improvements to it. They waited a while for these to be finished, enduring the customary thousand disappointments and delays caused by the workmen’s inexplicable slowness. Then Elinor, following the usual practice, abandoned the original firm decision that they would not marry until everything was ready, and the wedding took place in Barton church early that autumn.

They spent the first month of their marriage with their friend at the great house. From there they could watch the work at the parsonage and give their instructions on the spot, choosing wallpapers, planning shrubberies, and devising a curved drive. Though Mrs. Jennings had confused some of the details, most of her predictions came true: by Michaelmas she was able to visit Edward and his wife in their parsonage, and she found Elinor and her husband, as she sincerely believed, among the happiest married couples in the world. In fact they had only two remaining wishes: that Colonel Brandon should marry Marianne, and that their cows should have rather better grazing.

Nearly all their relations and friends visited them when they first settled in. Mrs. Ferrars came to examine the happiness she was almost ashamed of having permitted; even the Dashwoods paid for a journey from Sussex in order to honour them with a visit.

“I shall not say I am disappointed, my dear sister,” John remarked as they walked together one morning outside the gates of Delaford House. “_That_ would be going too far, for you are certainly already one of the most fortunate young women in the world. Still, I admit that it would give me enormous pleasure to call Colonel Brandon my brother. His estate here, the grounds, the house—everything is so thoroughly respectable and in such excellent order! And the woods! Nowhere in Dorsetshire have I seen timber to compare with what is standing at this moment in Delaford Hanger! Perhaps Marianne does not seem exactly the sort of woman to attract him. Nevertheless, I think it would be altogether wise for you to have them both staying with you frequently now. Colonel Brandon appears to spend a great deal of time at home, and nobody can predict what might happen. When people are constantly together and have hardly anyone else to see—and you will always be able to show her to advantage, and so on. In short, you might as well give her the opportunity. You understand what I mean.”

Although Mrs. Ferrars _did_ visit them, and always put on a show of suitable affection, she never subjected them to the insult of her genuine favour or preference. _That_ belonged to Robert’s foolishness and his wife’s cunning, and within a few months they had earned it. The same shrewd pursuit of her own interests that had first drawn Robert into trouble was chiefly responsible for rescuing him from it. As soon as Lucy was given the slightest chance, her respectful submission, tireless attentions, and unending flattery reconciled Mrs. Ferrars to his choice and restored him completely to her good graces.

Lucy’s conduct throughout the affair, and the prosperity that rewarded it, may therefore be offered as a most encouraging example of what a serious and unflagging devotion to self-interest can achieve. However many obstacles seem to stand in its path, it can secure every advantage that money brings, at no greater cost than time and conscience. When Robert first made her acquaintance and visited her secretly in Bartlett’s Buildings, he had only the purpose his brother had attributed to him. He simply intended to persuade her to break the engagement. Since he had nothing to overcome beyond the affection of the two people concerned, he naturally supposed that one or two meetings would settle everything. On this point, and this point alone, he was mistaken. Lucy soon encouraged him to hope that his eloquence would persuade her _eventually_, but one further visit, one further conversation, was always needed to complete the persuasion. Whenever they parted, some doubts still remained in her mind, and only another half-hour’s discussion with him could remove them. In this way she secured his continued visits, and the rest followed naturally. Gradually, instead of discussing Edward, they discussed only Robert: a subject on which he always had more to say than on any other, and in which she soon showed an interest quite equal to his own. Before long, in short, both understood that he had entirely displaced his brother. He was proud of winning her, proud of outwitting Edward, and especially proud of marrying in secret without his mother’s permission. What happened immediately afterwards has already been related. They spent several very happy months at Dawlish, where she had numerous relations and old acquaintances to snub, and he drew several designs for magnificent cottages. Returning from there to London, they obtained Mrs. Ferrars’s forgiveness by the simple method of asking for it—a course they took at Lucy’s suggestion. At first, to be sure, and quite reasonably, the forgiveness extended only to Robert. Lucy, who had owed his mother no duty and consequently could have broken none, remained unforgiven for several weeks longer. But she persisted in humble behaviour and humble messages, blamed herself for Robert’s offence, and expressed gratitude for the unkind treatment she received. Eventually these efforts won her the condescending attention that overwhelmed her with its graciousness, and from there she quickly advanced to the highest degree of affection and influence. Mrs. Ferrars came to find Lucy as indispensable as either Robert or Fanny. Edward was never sincerely forgiven for once intending to marry her, while Elinor, though better born and wealthier than Lucy, was spoken of as an intruder; but _Lucy’s_ wishes were consulted in everything, and she was always openly acknowledged as a favourite child. They established themselves in London, received very generous financial help from Mrs. Ferrars, and enjoyed the best imaginable relations with the Dashwoods. Apart from the jealousy and hostility that constantly existed between Fanny and Lucy, in which their husbands naturally joined, and the frequent quarrels between Robert and Lucy themselves, no one could have lived together more harmoniously.

Many people might have struggled to discover what Edward had done to lose his privileges as the eldest son; what Robert had done to inherit them might have baffled them even more. Still, the results justified the arrangement, whatever might be said of its cause. Nothing in Robert’s conversation or way of life ever suggested that he regretted the size of his income, either because it left his brother too little or because it gave himself too much. As for Edward, anyone judging by his willing attention to every one of his duties, his growing attachment to his wife and home, and his steadily cheerful spirits might reasonably suppose him just as satisfied with his own share, and just as free from any desire to exchange it.

Elinor’s marriage separated her from her family as little as was possible without making the Barton cottage entirely unnecessary, for her mother and sisters spent considerably more than half their time with her. Mrs. Dashwood’s frequent visits to Delaford combined strategy with pleasure. Her wish to bring Marianne and Colonel Brandon together was scarcely less eager than John’s, though rather more generous in its motives. It was now her dearest ambition. Much as she treasured her daughter’s company, she wanted nothing so much as to surrender the pleasure of having it constantly herself to her valued friend. Edward and Elinor were equally anxious to see Marianne established in the great house. All three felt for his suffering, and felt their own debts to him; by common agreement, Marianne was to serve as the reward for everything.

With such an alliance working against her, with such intimate knowledge of his goodness, and with the certainty of his devoted love for her—a certainty that finally dawned on her long after everyone else had seen it—what could she possibly do?

Marianne Dashwood had been born for an extraordinary destiny. She was born to find her own opinions mistaken and to contradict, by her behaviour, the principles she cherished most. She was born to recover from a love formed at so advanced an age as seventeen, and freely to marry someone else while feeling nothing stronger than deep respect and warm friendship! And _that_ someone was a man who had suffered as severely as she had from an earlier love, whom she had thought too old to marry only two years before, and who still protected his health by wearing a flannel waistcoat!

Yet that was what happened. She did not become the victim of an irresistible passion, as she had once so fondly expected; nor did she remain with her mother for ever, finding all her pleasure in seclusion and study, as she had later resolved in a calmer and more sensible frame of mind. Instead, at nineteen she found herself accepting new affections and new responsibilities, established in a new home as a wife, the mistress of a household, and the benefactress of a village.

Colonel Brandon was now as happy as those who loved him best thought he deserved to be. Marianne comforted him for every past sorrow; her affection and companionship brought life back to his mind and cheerfulness to his spirits. Everyone close to them was equally convinced, and equally delighted to believe, that in making him happy Marianne had found her own happiness. She could never give only half her heart. In time she devoted it as completely to her husband as she had once devoted it to Willoughby.

Willoughby could not hear of her marriage without pain. Soon afterwards his punishment was completed when Mrs. Smith freely forgave him. She explained that she was being merciful because he had married a respectable woman, thereby giving him reason to believe that if he had behaved honourably towards Marianne, he might have secured both happiness and wealth. There is no need to doubt that he sincerely regretted misconduct which had brought its own punishment, or that he continued for a long time to envy Colonel Brandon and remember Marianne with regret. But no one should rely on his having remained inconsolable for ever, abandoned society, sunk into permanent gloom, or died of a broken heart: he did none of these things. He lived to occupy himself actively and, quite often, to enjoy himself. His wife was not invariably ill-tempered, and his home was not invariably unpleasant. His breeding of horses and dogs, and his enjoyment of every kind of field sport, supplied him with a considerable measure of domestic happiness.

Despite his discourtesy in surviving the loss of Marianne, however, he always kept a particular affection for her. It made him take an interest in everything that happened to her and privately regard her as the standard of perfection in a woman. In later years he would dismiss many a newly admired beauty as incapable of comparison with Mrs. Brandon.

Mrs. Dashwood had enough good sense to stay at the cottage, without trying to move to Delaford. Fortunately for Sir John and Mrs. Jennings, by the time Marianne was lost to their circle, Margaret had reached an age thoroughly suited to dancing, and quite suitable for being suspected of having an admirer.

Barton and Delaford remained in the constant contact that warm family affection would naturally inspire. And among Elinor’s and Marianne’s virtues and sources of happiness, this should count for no small amount: although they were sisters, and lived almost within sight of one another, they managed to avoid quarrelling themselves or creating any coolness between their husbands.
